source.title: For Interpolating Kernel Machines, Minimizing the Norm of the ERM Solution Maximizes Stability
source.authors: Akshay Rangamani; L. Rosasco; T. Poggio

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses and predicts a double-descent pattern under assumptions, but does not itself test the claim's model-size, epoch, sample-size, or other stated curves. Its own simulation varies the norm of interpolating solutions instead.
record.gate_note: The paper's condition-number curves in Figures 2 and 3 are attributed to Poggio et al. (2019), so they are not recorded as this study's results. Its theoretical prediction of double descent is not an empirical test. The paper's own simulation reports a qualitative test-MSE result for interpolating solutions, recorded under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The paper derives CVloo stability bounds for ridgeless kernel and linear least squares. It argues that, under random-kernel assumptions, test error should follow a double descent curve, but it reports no own test-error curve over size, samples, epochs or capacity. The condition-number and pseudoinverse-norm double-descent figures (Figs 2, 3) are reproduced from Poggio et al. (2019) and measure a matrix quantity, not test error. Its only own experiment varies the norm of interpolants at fixed n=200, d=1000, which is not an axis in any version. Treated as theoretical discussion (T6) rather than a test.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors show that the minimum-norm interpolant minimizes an upper bound on CVloo stability. That bound, and hence the excess-risk bound, is controlled by the kernel-matrix condition number. They argue this can account for double descent in kernel interpolants under appropriate distributional assumptions (random kernel matrices), linking numerical and statistical stability. They also note the result applies to gradient descent, which converges to the minimum-norm solution.
record.recipe_differences: The paper develops stability bounds for ridgeless kernel and linear least squares and includes a synthetic comparison across interpolant norms; it does not sweep model size, epochs, or sample size to measure a double-descent curve.

fits_no_version.finding: In a synthetic linear regression (d=1000, n=200, 100 trials), all interpolants reach zero train MSE. Test MSE rises as the interpolant's distance from the minimum-norm solution grows.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Among interpolating least-squares solutions, the minimum-norm interpolant has the lowest test error, and test error grows with distance from it.

fits_no_version.finding: Theoretical result: the excess-risk bound for the minimum-norm interpolant is controlled by the kernel-matrix condition number. Per cited prior work, the condition number itself peaks at n=d.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The double-descent peak at the interpolation threshold is tied to ill-conditioning of the kernel or data matrix (a theoretical bound, not a measured test-error curve).

record.problems: The own simulation reports a qualitative plot rather than numerical test-MSE values or uncertainty estimates. Its condition-number double-descent figures are credited to prior work, not presented as this study's own results.
record.rows_left_out: No own-result rows were omitted. Figures 2 and 3 are attributed to Poggio et al. (2019), and cited findings in the related-work discussion were excluded.

untested.parts: No sweep of model size in deep networks.
No test error over training epochs.
No test error measured as sample size varies. Only a cited condition-number curve over n is shown.
No own measurement of risk across capacity for kernel or linear models. Double descent is only predicted from a bound plus cited random-matrix results.
No test of whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak location. The condition-number link is a bound, not a measured prediction.
No label-noise, multiple-peak or tuned-regularization experiments.

record.verdict_notes: Figures 2 and 3 are credited to Poggio et al. (2019) and show double descent of the condition number or pseudoinverse norm versus n, not of test error, so correctly no rows. The double-descent statement is a prediction derived from an upper bound plus cited asymptotics, not an empirical test. Peer-reviewed venue as recorded.

versions.untested_parts: Model-size sweep and peak near the interpolation threshold.
Changing training sample size near the interpolation threshold.
An own-result test of risk across capacity in kernel or other model classes.
Whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak location across size, epochs, and samples.
Noise, multiple peaks, and optimally tuned regularization.
Whether effective-parameter counting turns the second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.
